1.pericope_label: In the beginning God created: the heaven and the earth, and the Spirit upon the waters

schools.summary: Gill reports the dispute over the heaven, some understanding the heaven of heavens, the habitation of God and the angels, made perfect at once and therefore not mentioned again, with the angels created then since they were present at the laying of the foundations, though he prefers the lower and visible heavens; on the formlessness he holds that the earth had a form as all matter must but not the form it now has, the watery parts unseparated from the earthy, and cites the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem for a waste and desert. Calvin declines to be very solicitous about the two epithets, which the Hebrews use of anything empty and confused or vain, and sets them in opposition to everything that pertains to the form, the ornament and the perfection of the world.

Henry keeps to the visible creation, calling the world a great house of upper and lower stories, stately and uniform, with every room well and wisely furnished, and noting that the creation of angels is passed over because it is the visible part that Moses designs to account for; he finds in the verse the first article of the creed, that God the Father Almighty is Maker of heaven and earth, and takes these two verses for the work of creation in its epitome and in its embryo.

Ellicott denies that in the beginning here means from eternity as it does in John, taking it of the beginning of this sidereal system, and holds that since there was never a time when God did not exist there was probably never a time when worlds did not exist, God calling them into being when and how he willed; he explains Elohim as plural in form but joined with a singular verb, its root-meaning strength, and refuses the plural of majesty, taking it for the effort of early human thought feeling after the Deity and concluding that the Deity is one. He insists too on the conjunction of the second verse, which defeats the attempt to harmonise geology and Scripture by treating the first verse as a heading, since the two go together as a summary afterwards divided into stages, and presses the verb as the substantive verb existed, expressing duration. Keil and Delitzsch note that the writer describes with minuteness only the original condition and progressive formation of the earth, saying no more of the heaven than is necessary.

Clarke reports the two Hebrew words for the formlessness as of uncertain etymology but conveying everywhere the idea of confusion and disorder, thinks the ancient Syrians and Egyptians borrowed their gods Theuth and Bau from them and the Greeks their Chaos, and supposes that God first created the elementary principles. Wesley notes that Moses designs to account only for the visible creation and that even in it there are secrets which cannot be fathomed, names the two things the second verse gives as the first matter and the first Mover, and observes that the chaos is called the earth though the earth properly taken was not made until the third day, because it most resembled what was afterwards so called, and is called the deep both for its vastness and because the waters afterwards separated were then mixed with it.

Basil the Great sets the tone of his own commentary rather than expounding a clause: it is right that one beginning to narrate the formation of the world should begin with the good order reigning in visible things, and the creation of heaven and earth was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God. He asks what ear is worthy to hear such a tale, and on the second verse continues in the same key, that if the fore court of the sanctuary is so grand and the splendour of its portico so dazzles the eyes of the soul, one may hardly dare look into the holy of holies; yet since rewards are reserved for the intention alone of doing good he will not hesitate to continue, hoping with the help of the Spirit not to fall away from the meaning of Holy Scripture.

debates: Whether the first verse is a heading or part of the narrative: Ellicott says the conjunction of the second verse defeats the reading of the first as a mere heading offered to harmonise geology with Scripture, the two verses forming one summary afterwards divided into stages

What the heaven of the first verse is: Gill reports those who take it for the heaven of heavens, made perfect at once and never mentioned again, with the angels created then, but prefers the lower and visible heavens, as Henry and Wesley also confine the account to the visible creation
outliers: Ellicott holds that there was probably never a time when worlds did not exist, since activity is essential to the being of God, and that creation may have proceeded by a universal law of which God is himself the author
Clarke derives the Syrian and Egyptian gods Theuth and Bau, and the Greek Chaos, from the two Hebrew words rendered without form and void

The most vivid gloss on the Spirit moving, a continued brooding as of a fowl hatching eggs, belongs to a block the scrapers filed one verse late and which is therefore excluded from the entry that carries it

3.pericope_label: Let there be light: the first day, its division and its naming

schools.summary: Gill notes that the phrase God said occurs nine times in the account and that Longinus the heathen admired it in his treatise on the sublime, takes the goodness of the light as foreseen rather than experienced since no inhabitants were yet there to profit by it, and explains the vicissitude of day and night by the circling of that body of light or the rotation of the chaos on its own axis. Calvin uses the same clause against a different error, that Moses now for the first time introduces God speaking, as if he had created heaven and earth without the Word, whereas John testifies that without him nothing was made that was made; he insists that God is introduced surveying his work for our sake, to teach us that he made nothing without reason and design, and allows the last clause a double interpretation, whether the evening and morning belonged to the first day or the first day consisted of them.

Henry holds that the first of all visible beings created was light, the great beauty and blessing of the universe, which like the first-born most resembles its great parent in purity and power, brightness and beneficence; it was made not that God might see to work, since darkness and light are both alike to him, but that we might see his works and work our own while it is day. He adds that the works of Satan are works of darkness while he who does truth comes to the light, and that light is of such affinity with spirit that though we are sure it is, we cannot describe its nature.

Ellicott makes the phrase God said metaphorical, since there could be neither voice nor sound nor any person addressed, and takes it to mean that God enacted a law for the universe, the sublimity lying in this, that God makes no preparation, employs no means and needs no secondary agency; on the approval he finds two things indicated, a lapse of time and a verdict of the divine reason, and observes that light was as indispensable for what followed as it was a necessary result of motion in the world-mass. He argues too that before day and night were possible there must have been outside the earth, not yet the sun but a bright phosphorescent mass such as now enwraps that luminary, and the earth must have begun to revolve. Keil and Delitzsch describe the word going forth to the primary material to call into being the creatures which proclaim their Creator's glory, defend the wording of the approval against the charge of anthropomorphism since man's seeing has its type in God's, and cite Augustine that all light is not day nor all darkness night but light and darkness alternating in regular order constitute them.

Clarke gives the Hebrew and says nothing can be conceived more dignified than the form of the divine word, which argues at once uncontrollable authority and omnific power, so that in human language it is scarcely possible to conceive that God should speak more like himself, and reports that the Greek of the Septuagint fell in the way of Longinus; he denies that the dividing implies two distinct substances, darkness being only the privation of light, and refers the words by anticipation to the rotation of the earth on its axis once in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes and four seconds. Wesley agrees with Henry almost word for word on the light as the great beauty and blessing of the universe, and notes that it was made by the word of God's power alone.

debates: Whether the goodness of the light is foreseen or present: Gill takes it as foreseen, no inhabitants being yet there to profit by it, while Ellicott finds in the approval both a lapse of time and a verdict of the divine reason, and Calvin insists the survey is recorded for our sake and not because God learned anything by it

How day and night were possible before the sun: Clarke refers the division by anticipation to the earth's rotation, Ellicott posits a bright phosphorescent mass outside the earth together with the beginning of rotation, and Gill allows either the circling of that body of light or the rotation of the chaos
outliers: Both Gill and Clarke record that the Greek of this verse was singled out by the heathen critic Longinus in his treatise on the sublime
Keil and Delitzsch cite Augustine that all light is not day nor all darkness night, but that light and darkness alternating in a regular order constitute them
The Jamieson block filed at this verse belongs to the previous one, glossing without form and void and the Spirit brooding as a fowl over eggs, and is excluded here as misplaced

6.pericope_label: The firmament of the second day: the expanse, the waters above, and the naming of heaven

schools.summary: Gill takes the word as something stretched out and spread like a curtain, tent or canopy, to which all the passages on the stretching out of the heavens refer, and derives the name heaven either from its height or from a compound meaning there are waters. Calvin says he knows not why the Greeks chose their rendering, since the Hebrew comprehends whatever is open above us; against those who allegorize the waters above into angels he insists that nothing is here treated of but the visible form of the world, that he who would learn astronomy must go elsewhere, and that the history of the creation is the book of the unlearned, so that the waters meant are the clouds which threaten to fall upon our heads and yet leave us space to breathe. He accounts for the missing verdict of approval by there being no advantage from the work until the waters were gathered on the following day.

Henry describes the expansion as a sheet spread or a curtain drawn out, including all that is visible above the earth, as high as the place where the stars are fixed and as low as where the birds fly. He observes that between heaven and earth there is an inconceivable distance but no impassable gulf as there is between heaven and hell, so that the firmament is not a wall of partition but a way of intercourse; and that lest it seem God had only commanded the work and another had done it, Moses adds that God made it, for what God requires of us he himself works in us, or it is not done. The design is to distinguish the waters wrapped up in the clouds from those that cover the sea.

Clarke holds that the translators, by following the Vulgate rendering of the Septuagint word, have deprived the passage of all sense and meaning, the Hebrew signifying simply an expanse, the space separating the clouds above from the seas below, which we call the atmosphere, though Moses appears to use it more widely still, taking in the whole solar system. Wesley follows Henry closely on the expansion, its extent, its design of dividing the waters in the air from those in the earth, and its naming.

Keil and Delitzsch derive the noun from a verb meaning to stretch or spread out, and grant that appearance describes it as a carpet spread above the earth, a curtain, a transparent work of sapphire or a molten looking-glass, while denying that these poetical similes warrant the idea of a solid mass such as the Greek poets describe. Ellicott takes the contrary view of the ancient sense, that the word undoubtedly meant something solid to Greeks and probably to Hebrews and appears so in the poetry of Scripture, but that here, in sober language rather than vivid metaphor, it means an expanse; he finds the description of the waters above in accordance with science, the atmosphere being the receptacle of the waters evaporated from earth and ocean, and supposes the missing verdict of approval to mean that the second and third days are regarded as one work.

Basil opens his homily on this day by refusing to take from the first day the privilege of having been a day apart, not counted in the same order as the others, and praises not the talent of the narrator but the grace of Scripture, whose narrative is so naturally told that it delights all the friends of truth.

debates: Whether the firmament was conceived as solid: Ellicott holds that the word undoubtedly meant something solid to the Greeks and probably to the Hebrews, Keil and Delitzsch deny that the poetical similes warrant any such idea, and Clarke charges the Latin and Greek renderings with depriving the passage of all sense

Why this day alone lacks the verdict that it was good: Calvin supposes no advantage came of the work until the waters were gathered on the next day, where the note is twice repeated, while Ellicott takes the second and third days to be regarded as a single work of separation
outliers: Calvin sets aside astronomy and the recondite arts as beside the purpose here, on the ground that the Spirit would teach all men without exception and the history of the creation is the book of the unlearned
Henry turns the plain statement that God made the firmament into a rule of grace, that what God requires of us he himself works in us, or it is not done

9.pericope_label: The third day: the gathering of the waters, the appearing of the dry land, and the earth made fruitful

schools.summary: Calvin calls the retreat of the waters an illustrious miracle, since philosophers allow that water naturally covered the whole earth, and that the seas should be heaped up to give place for man is seemingly preternatural. He holds that herbs and trees were made before the sun and moon deliberately, so that we might learn to refer all things to God, since we confess the First Cause self-sufficient in words yet picture him as poor without second causes; and he finds in the words a power of propagation given with the first creation, that the species might be perpetuated. Gill has the waters flowing as by a straight line to the place broken up for them, perhaps by thunder and an earthquake which made the cavity of the sea and threw up the hills, derives the name of the earth from its being low and depressed, and closes on the chronologists who differ whether this day fell in spring or in autumn.

Henry observes that the seas, though many and in distant regions, communicate above ground or under ground and so are one, the common receptacle into which all the rivers run. He notes that the earth existed already but was of no use while under water, and draws from it that many of God’s gifts are received in vain because they are buried. From the fruitfulness of the earth before the sun he concludes that common providence is a continued creation, and that though God ordinarily makes use of second causes he neither needs them nor is tied to them.

Clarke cites Dr Long, who separated the land from the sea on the papers covering a seventeen-inch globe and weighed them, finding nearly three-fourths of the surface water, and defends that share by experiments on evaporation; he takes the oblate figure of the globe, conjectured by Newton and afterwards confirmed by measurement, to bear out the Mosaic account of a terraqueous mass created fluid. On the seed in itself he instances the elm, which produces one thousand five hundred and eighty-four millions of seeds, each with the same power, and asks who can comprehend the structure of a single plant. Wesley follows Henry on the unity of the seas and on the provision made both for the present and for time to come.

Ellicott takes the verb of condensation rather than gathering, impossible until the surface had been cooled by radiation, and describes the mass of water hitherto existing only as vapour, the stiffening crust ruptured from within along lines trending north-east to south-west, whence mountain ranges and deep sea beds. He makes the vegetation gradual and in three stages, a mere greenness without visible seed or stalk such as is still seen on rocks, then the seed-bearing plants and chiefly the cerealia, then the tree with woody stem, and can scarcely suppose fruit-trees existed before the sun shone. Keil and Delitzsch mark the day as the stage in which the earth was clothed with vegetation and fitted to be the abode of living beings.

Basil hears in the command to the earth a natural and permanent law, which gave it fertility and the power to produce fruit for all ages to come, and traces the stages of growth by which the germs begin to sprout and form grass, the plant insensibly receives its different articulations, and the whole reaches its maturity in the seed.

debates: Whether vegetation before the sun is a deliberate suspension of second causes or an ordinary development: Calvin and Henry take God to have withheld the instruments so that we might refer the earth’s fruitfulness to him alone, while Ellicott holds the record itself to describe a gradual growth and can scarcely suppose fruit-trees preceded the sunshine

How the waters were gathered: Gill supposes thunder and an earthquake breaking open the bed of the sea, Ellicott the condensation of vapour upon a cooling crust ruptured from within by an inner tidal wave, and Calvin an act seemingly preternatural which Scripture extols as a mercy to man
outliers: Clarke reports Dr Long weighing the separated land and sea papers of a seventeen-inch globe to establish the proportion of water to dry land
Gill notes that the chronologists place this day in April or in October according as they suppose the world made in spring or in autumn, and that the Jewish authorities are themselves divided
The Keil and Delitzsch material filed at this point is the opening of their section on the fourth day, their comment on the third day standing with the previous verses

14.pericope_label: The fourth day: the luminaries, their offices, and the manner in which Moses describes them

schools.summary: Calvin holds that God had already created the light and now institutes a new order in nature, ordaining instruments to diffuse the light already made, which was before dispersed and now proceeds from lucid bodies. He makes this the clearest case of accommodation in the chapter: Moses does not descant as a philosopher on the secrets of nature but writes in a popular style what all persons of common sense can understand, whereas astronomers prove that Saturn is greater than the moon; the question is not how great the sun is but how much light comes to us, and astronomy itself is not to be reprobated. Gill reports that some understand the words of the luminaries' appearance rather than their formation, judges rather that the light of the first day was now distributed into luminous bodies, gives the sun's measurements from Derham and Newton, and turns the making into a rebuke of idolaters who worship what God created for the use of men.

Henry states the governing principle of the day, that the lights are accounted for not as they are in themselves and in their own nature, to satisfy the curious, but as they stand in relation to this earth, to which they serve as lights, and that this is enough to furnish matter for praise and thanksgiving; though heaven is high it has respect to this earth, and should therefore have respect from it.

Clarke defends the phrase two great lights by observing that Moses speaks not of bulk or solid contents but of the proportion of light shed upon the earth, and that the moon, small as it is, affords more light to the earth than all the planets and stars together; he also explains how lights can divide the night, the rays diffused beyond the earth falling upon the opaque disc of the moon and being reflected back upon the hemisphere opposite the sun. Wesley calls the earlier light a chaos of light, scattered and confused, now collected into luminaries and so rendered both more glorious and more serviceable, and lists their uses for the distinction of times and the direction of actions, as signs of the weather by which the husbandman may order his affairs.

Ellicott rests the distinction on the Hebrew, which has one word for light and another for a light-bearer: the concentration of light into great centres began at once, and there was daylight long before this day, but only now did the sun and moon become fully formed and shine regularly in the bright sky. On the closing clause he corrects the English, since the sense is not that God then created the stars but that these too were to rule the night, and by them the planets are chiefly meant, so that only on this day was the solar system complete.

Basil opens his homily with the circus, where the laws require the spectator to sit bare-headed so that he may be not merely a spectator of the athletes but in some measure an athlete himself; so in contemplating the great show of creation his hearers must bring their own light to the work and are not so much judges as fellow combatants.

debates: Whether the luminaries were created on this day or only then appeared: Gill records the view that only their appearance is meant and prefers that the light of the first day was now gathered into bodies, Calvin has God ordaining new instruments for light already made, and Ellicott has the sun and moon becoming fully formed and regularly visible only now

How far the language is to be pressed against astronomy: Calvin makes the popular style deliberate and defends astronomy as a separate study, Clarke answers the objection about the moon by distinguishing bulk from light shed, while Gill supplies the measured diameters and bulk of the sun
outliers: Gill cites Derham's computation of the sun's diameter and Newton's estimate of its bulk in the middle of a comment on the folly of worshipping it
Basil compares his hearers to spectators at the circus who are required to sit bare-headed, and tells them they are not judges but fellow combatants

20.pericope_label: The fifth day and the beasts of the sixth: the waters peopled, the blessing of increase, and the earth bringing forth

schools.summary: Calvin raises the difficulty that the word created is used here of things formed from other matter, rejects as a subterfuge the plea that the fishes were properly created because the waters could not produce them, and refers the creation spoken of to the shapeless mass which was the fountain of the whole world. On the benediction he holds that God does not pray for a blessing after the manner of men but effects by the bare intimation of his purpose what men seek by entreaty, and that the word addressed to the fishes was not transient but took root in their nature. At the sixth day he asks whence a dead element has life, and finds the miracle as great as a creation out of nothing. Gill collects the ancients on the size of whales, one in the Indian sea five times bigger than the largest elephant and, on the authority of Juba, some six hundred feet long, and notes that the heathen had a traditionary notion of the earth bringing forth, reported of the Egyptians by Diodorus.

Henry observes that the work of creation not only proceeded gradually from one thing to another but advanced from the less excellent to the more so, teaching us to press towards perfection and to endeavour that our last works may be our best works; fish and fowl were made together and both out of the waters, since the power of the first Cause can produce very different effects from the same second causes. At the sixth day he denies that the earth had any prolific virtue of its own or that God resigned his creating power to it, the creatures being made of divers shapes and also of divers natures, manners, food and fashions.

Clarke takes the word rendered whales as a general rather than a particular term, comprising the whale, the porpoise, the dolphin, the narwal and the shark, and observes that God delights to show himself in the little as in the great, naturalists having found not less than thirty thousand animalcula in a single drop of water, each a perfect animal furnished with bones, muscles, nerves and viscera. On the fecundity of fishes he reports a tench laying a thousand eggs, a carp twenty thousand, and Leeuwenhoek counting more than nine million in a middling cod. Wesley follows Henry on the gradual advance of the work and on the making of the beasts after their kind.

Ellicott sets the fifth day in the correspondence of the two creative triads, light created on the first day and gathered into light-bearers on the fourth, air and water called into being on the second and peopled on the fifth, the dry land appearing on the third and becoming the home of animals and man on the sixth. He renders the command literally as a swarming of living soul, the word soul properly signifying breath; holds that the Hebrew for whales means any long creature, used of serpents, the crocodile and sea monsters, and so marks the great Saurian age; and finds in the blessing evidence that the earth was replenished from a limited number of progenitors. Keil and Delitzsch divide the living beings of the sixth day into three classes.

Basil describes the peopling of the waters as the completing of an adornment, earth having received hers from her own plants and the heavens the flowers of the stars, with the two great luminaries beautifying them like two eyes; at the command the rivers and lakes became fruitful, the sea travailed, and not even in mud and marshes did the water remain idle. Against the Manichaeans, whom he calls mad-minded for giving the earth a soul, he holds that at the word the earth did not produce a germ contained in it, but that he who gave the order at the same time gifted it with the grace and power to bring forth.

debates: What the word created can mean where the material already existed: Calvin refuses the plea that the waters were insufficient and carries the word back to the original mass, while Ellicott attaches it not to the sea monsters but to the whole verse as describing the introduction of animal life

Whether the earth brought forth of itself: Calvin, Henry and Gill deny it any prolific virtue, Basil answers the Manichaeans that the power to bring forth was given with the command, and Ellicott holds that the phrase, though it literally means spontaneous generation, need mean no more than that land animals followed those produced in the waters
outliers: Gill assembles ancient reports of whales from Aelian, Theocles, Pliny and Juba, including one said to have taken up four acres of land
Clarke supports the fecundity of fishes with Leeuwenhoek’s count of more than nine million eggs in a middling cod

26.pericope_label: The making of man: the divine consultation, the image and likeness, dominion and the blessing

schools.summary: Gill rejects in turn the readings that God addressed the earth, which he calls wretchedly stupid, that he addressed the angels, who are not of his privy council, and that he used a plural of majesty, since that manner of speech did not obtain so early; the words are spoken by the Father to the Son and the Holy Ghost. He places the image in the erect stature of the body, the immortality of the soul, the intellectual powers, the righteousness in which man was created, and the dominion in which he was God’s viceregent. Calvin argues the same case more fiercely, that the earth was no adviser and that to ascribe any part of the work to angels is a sacrilege, and infers from God summoning no foreign counsellor that he finds within himself something distinct. He reads the consultation as a tribute to the excellency of man, whom the ancients deservedly called a world in miniature, finds in male and female a commendation of the conjugal bond implying that the man alone was incomplete, and takes the blessing as the fountain from which the race has flowed, God willing that we should proceed from one source so that our desire of mutual concord might be the greater.

Henry has the three persons consulting and concurring in the making of man, because man when made was to be devoted to Father, Son and Holy Ghost. He observes that man was made last so that it might not be suspected he had been any way a helper in the creation, yet that the lateness was both an honour, the method being to advance from the less perfect to the more so, and a favour, since it was not fit he should be lodged in the palace designed for him until it was furnished for his reception. Image and likeness he makes two words for one thing, warning that between God and man there is an infinite distance and that man bears the image only as the shadow in the glass or the king’s impress upon the coin, the soul in its understanding, will and active power being the brightest looking-glass in nature wherein to see God.

Clarke argues that God, being infinite, is neither limited by parts nor definable by passions, so that the likeness must be intellectual, God being the fountain whence this spirit issued and the stream resembling the spring; the image, as Paul defines it, consisted in righteousness, true holiness and knowledge, so that man was wise in his mind, holy in his heart and righteous in his actions. He cites Gregory of Nyssa that all other creatures are represented as the effect of God’s word but man as the work of God, according to plan and consideration, and denies that the dominion was the image, God having created man capable of governing the world and then fixed him in the office. Wesley follows Henry on the honour and favour of man being made last and on the turning of the word of command into a word of consultation.

Ellicott is more guarded on the plural, noting that Maimonides took God to have consulted the earth and the Jewish interpreters generally the angels, and holding that in the name Elohim, many powers concentrated in one being, lies the germ of a plurality of persons in the divine Unity, though this is not a formal proof of the Trinity and believers in the inspiration of Scripture do not so use it. He divides the two terms, the image referring to reason, free will and self-consciousness and the likeness to man’s moral powers and capacity of attaining unto holiness, both weakened by the fall yet retained in some degree and both perfect in the man Christ Jesus; the body he allows to be after God’s image only as the means whereby man attains dominion. The plural in the grant of dominion he takes to show that the race and not the individual pair is in view, and the thrice-repeated verb created to mark something in man that was not a development.

debates: Whom the plural addresses: Gill and Calvin take it of the Father speaking to the Son and the Spirit and reject the earth, the angels and the plural of majesty outright, while Ellicott records the Jewish readings and finds here only the germ of the doctrine, expressly denying that it is a formal proof of the Trinity

Whether dominion belongs to the image: Clarke says plainly that the dominion was not the image but a consequence of it, Ellicott makes the body God’s image only as the instrument of rule, and Gill counts the dominion itself part of the resemblance
outliers: Calvin reports the older opinion that man is a world in miniature, so exact a specimen is he of divine wisdom, justice and goodness
Clarke appeals to Gregory of Nyssa for the observation that the other creatures are made by a word while man is made by counsel

29.pericope_label: The provision of food and the final verdict: every herb given for meat, and behold it was very good

schools.summary: Gill observes that the grant of food is spoken to Adam and Eve, to whom the dominion had been given, and that the beasts of the earth, wild or tame, are provided for as being all God’s creatures and designed to answer some end of their creation. On the closing review he holds that the survey is attributed to God after the manner of men, as workmen look over their work to see whether anything is amiss or wanting, not that anything of the kind can be supposed in the works of God, but to show their completeness and excellency, and he records that Picherellus would limit the review to the work of this day alone. Calvin makes the same concession about the manner of speech and draws a rule from it, that the Lord designed his judgment to be an example to us so that none should dare think or speak otherwise of his works; he finds in the sixfold repetition a bridle upon the temerity of man, and takes the final verdict to mark the highest perfection in the symmetry of God’s works, to which nothing can be added.

Henry takes the herbs and fruits as man’s appointed meat, including corn and all the products of the earth, flesh not being allowed until after the flood, and adds that before the earth was deluged, much more before it was cursed for man’s sake, its fruits were more pleasing to the taste and more nourishing than marrow and fatness are now. From the review he argues that all the works of God’s hands are under his eye, that he who made all sees all, that omniscience cannot be separated from omnipotence, and that God has hereby set us an example of reviewing our own works, communing with our hearts at the end of a day’s work, of a week’s, and of a life’s.

Clarke reports Priestley’s inference that man was originally intended to live upon vegetables only, and that since no change was made in the structure of men’s bodies after the flood no change is likely to have been made in their food; from the same silence it may be inferred that no animal was designed to prey on others, since nothing is given to any beast besides green herbs. He holds that before sin entered the world there could be at least no violent deaths, if any death at all, but that by the structure of the teeth of animals God prepared them for the aliment they were to subsist on after the Fall; and he reads the closing Hebrew as superlatively or only good, everything formed to the utmost perfection of its nature. Wesley asks whether God takes care of oxen and answers that the young lions and young ravens also ask and have their meat from him, and distinguishes the two verdicts, since each day’s work but the second was good while the whole together is very good.

Ellicott sorts the grant by the classes of plants named earlier, the two more perfect kinds being given to man while the birds and beasts receive every green herb, so that the fundamental supply of animal life is the blade and leaf and that of human life the perfected seed and ripe fruit; man is thus marked from the first as of a higher organisation, and the fact that his food requires preparation and cooking has been the basis not only of most of the refinements of life but of the close union of the family. He agrees that the food originally assigned was vegetable and that express leave to eat flesh came only after the flood, yet holds the dominion already granted had made it lawful to use the animals. The final blessing upon the completed work of the Friday he sets beside the last words of Christ spoken of the second creation on the same day of the week, and he holds the verdict to have respect to man as a species and so not to be annulled by the fall.

debates: Whether the original grant excludes the death of animals: Clarke, following Priestley, infers from the silence that no animal was designed to prey on others and that there could be no violent death before sin, while allowing that the structure of their teeth was a preparation for what came after the Fall; Ellicott holds that the dominion already granted made the use of animals lawful from the first, though express leave to eat flesh waited for the flood

What the divine review amounts to: Gill and Calvin agree that it is spoken after the manner of men and deny any real inspection, Gill adding the opinion of Picherellus that only this day’s work is in view, while Henry treats it as a pattern set for our own self-examination
outliers: Ellicott makes the need to cook human food the basis not only of the refinements of life but of the family itself, asking what would become of it without the common meal
Calvin reads the sixfold repetition of the divine approval as so many bridles laid upon the restless audacity of man
